l: Mormon, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 18
s: Mormon was the place where Alma taught believers and where about two hundred and four people were baptized. It contained a fountain of pure water, a thicket where Alma hid, and a forest near the waters.

l: waters of Mormon, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 18
s: The waters of Mormon were the place where Alma baptized about two hundred and four people. Alma described them, the forest, and the place of Mormon as beautiful to those who came to know their Redeemer.

l: wilderness, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 18
s: The wilderness was the destination to which Alma and the people departed with their tents and families. They left Mormon to avoid the coming army of king Noah.

l: the first resurrection, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 18
s: The resurrection of the dead was among the teachings Alma received from Abinadi and taught to the people. Those who entered the covenant were promised to be numbered with those of the first resurrection.

l: redemption, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 18
s: Redemption was taught as coming through the power, sufferings, death, resurrection, and ascension of Christ. Alma preached repentance and redemption, and the people sought to be redeemed of God.

l: repentance, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 18
s: Alma repented of his sins and iniquities. He taught the people repentance and commanded the priests to preach repentance and faith on the Lord.

l: faith, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 18
s: Alma taught faith on the Lord as part of the message given to the people. The church was commanded to have one faith.

l: baptism, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 18
s: Alma baptized Helam and the other believers in the waters of Mormon. Baptism served as a witness before God that they had entered a covenant to serve him and keep his commandments.

l: covenant, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 18
s: The people desired to enter the fold of God and be called his people. Through baptism, they entered a covenant to serve God and keep his commandments until death.

l: commandments, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 18
s: The people covenanted to keep God’s commandments. Alma also commanded them to avoid contention, observe the sabbath, give thanks, share their substance, and support those in need.

l: king's accusation of rebellion, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 18
s: The king accused Alma of stirring up the people to rebellion against him. Because of this accusation, he sent his army to destroy Alma and the people.

l: departure into the wilderness, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 18
s: Alma and the people were informed that the king’s army was coming to destroy them. They took their tents and families and departed into the wilderness, numbering about four hundred and fifty souls.

l: knowledge of the Redeemer, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 18
s: The place of Mormon, its waters, and its forest were described as beautiful to those who came there to the knowledge of their Redeemer. Those who gained this knowledge were described as blessed and as singing to his praise forever.

l: The Book of Mosiah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 19
s: The army of the king returns after searching unsuccessfully for the people of the Lord, but division and contention arise among the remaining people. Gideon attacks king Noah, who escapes when the Lamanites invade from the land of Shemlon and leads the people into the wilderness. The Lamanites capture many of king Noah’s people, spare them after their fair daughters plead for them, and impose tribute while requiring king Noah’s surrender. After king Noah is killed and his priests flee, Limhi becomes king, establishes peace, and rules for two years under Lamanite guards and tribute.

l: king Noah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 19
s: King Noah flees from Gideon by climbing a tower when Gideon is about to slay him. He leads his people into the wilderness during the Lamanite attack, commands the men to leave their wives and children, and is later captured by his people and killed by fire.

l: Gideon, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 19
s: Gideon, a strong man and enemy of the king, fights king Noah and pursues him to the tower. He spares king Noah when the Lamanites appear, later sends men to search for him, and learns what happened to the people and their king.

l: Limhi, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 19
s: Limhi, a son of king Noah, is taken captive with the people and desires that his father not be destroyed, although he knows his father’s iniquities. The people confer the kingdom upon him, and he establishes the kingdom and peace among his people.

l: king of the Lamanites, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 19
s: The king of the Lamanites makes an oath that his people will not slay Limhi’s people. He receives their tribute, places guards around their land, and supports the guards from the tribute.

l: Lamanites, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 19
s: The Lamanites enter the borders of the land of Shemlon, pursue king Noah’s people into the wilderness, and begin to slay them. They have compassion on those whose fair daughters plead with them, take the people captive, return them to the land of Nephi, and grant them possession of the land under conditions.

l: Nephites, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 19
s: The Nephites are identified as the people who must pay one half of all they possess to the king of the Lamanites. They remain in the land under Lamanite guards.

l: land of Nephi, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 19
s: The Lamanites carry the captured people back to the land of Nephi. The people return there after learning that their wives and children were not slain.

l: tribute to the king of the Lamanites, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 19
s: The tribute consists of one half of all the people possess, including one half of their gold, silver, and precious things. It is paid from year to year and supports the guards whom the king of the Lamanites sets around the land.

l: invasion of the land of Shemlon, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 19
s: The army of the Lamanites comes within the borders of the land of Shemlon while Gideon is pursuing king Noah. The invasion causes king Noah and his people to flee into the wilderness.

l: flight into the wilderness, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 19
s: King Noah commands the people to flee before the Lamanites, and they leave with their women and children. He later commands the men to leave their families, causing some to flee while others remain with their families.

l: capture of king Noah's people, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 19
s: The Lamanites overtake king Noah’s people and begin to slay them. They spare those whose fair daughters plead for them, take them captive, and grant them possession of the land under tribute and the condition that they deliver up king Noah.

l: death of king Noah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 19
s: King Noah’s people find him in the wilderness without his priests. After he commands them not to return, they become angry and cause him to suffer death by fire.

l: establishment of Limhi's kingdom, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 19
s: The people confer the kingdom upon Limhi after returning to the land of Nephi. Limhi begins to establish the kingdom while his people pay tribute to the king of the Lamanites.

l: peace among Limhi's people, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 19
s: Limhi begins to establish peace among his people. They have continual peace in the kingdom for two years, during which the Lamanites do not molest or seek to destroy them.

l: The Book of Mosiah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 20
s: In Shemlon, the priests of king Noah abduct twenty-four daughters of the Lamanites while they are gathered to sing and dance. The Lamanites blame the people of Limhi and attack them, but the people of Limhi defend themselves and capture the wounded king of the Lamanites. Limhi learns that the priests committed the abduction, and Gideon urges him to explain this to the king rather than punish his people. The king of the Lamanites is pacified, and both peoples meet without arms and return peacefully to their own lands.

l: land of Shemlon, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 20
s: Shemlon contains a place where the daughters of the Lamanites gather to sing, dance, and make themselves merry.

l: Lamanites, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 20
s: The Lamanites discover that their daughters are missing and blame the people of Limhi. They attack the people of Limhi, are defeated, and later become compassionate and pacified toward them.

l: the daughters of the Lamanites, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 20
s: The daughters of the Lamanites gather in Shemlon to sing and dance. Twenty-four of them are taken into the wilderness by the priests of king Noah.

l: priests of Noah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 20
s: The priests of king Noah remain in the wilderness because they fear returning to Nephi. They watch the daughters of the Lamanites and carry twenty-four of them into the wilderness.

l: wilderness, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 20
s: The priests of king Noah tarry in the wilderness after fleeing from Nephi. They discover the daughters of the Lamanites there and take them away.

l: king of the Lamanites, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 20
s: The king of the Lamanites leads his people against the people of Limhi, is wounded and captured, and learns that the priests caused the abduction. He is pacified and returns peacefully with his people.

l: the people of Limhi, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 20
s: The people of Limhi are attacked because the Lamanites think they abducted their daughters. They defend themselves, capture the wounded king, and meet the Lamanites without arms after the matter is explained.

l: Limhi, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 20
s: Limhi discovers the Lamanites' preparations for war and leads his people in defending themselves. He refuses to kill the captured king, searches for the truth, and explains the abduction to him.

l: war, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 20
s: War arises when the Lamanites attack the people of Limhi over the missing daughters. The conflict ends after the king of the Lamanites is pacified.

l: battle, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 20
s: The battle between the Lamanites and the people of Limhi becomes exceedingly sore. The people of Limhi drive the Lamanites back despite being fewer in number.

l: Gideon, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 20
s: Gideon, the king's captain, asks Limhi not to search and punish his people. He identifies the priests of king Noah as the abductors and urges Limhi to pacify the Lamanite king.

l: oath between the Lamanite king and Limhi, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 20
s: Limhi says that his people have not broken the oath made to the Lamanites. The king of the Lamanites breaks his oath by attacking because he believes the people of Limhi took the daughters.

l: Abinadi, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 20
s: Abinadi is remembered as having prophesied against the people because they would not hearken to the Lord's words and turn from their iniquities.

l: words of Abinadi, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 20
s: The words of Abinadi are said to be fulfilled through the people's suffering and the shedding of blood caused by their iniquities.

l: abduction of the daughters, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 20
s: The abduction of the daughters is carried out by the priests of king Noah, who take twenty-four daughters of the Lamanites into the wilderness. It causes the Lamanites to attack the people of Limhi.

l: Lamanite attack on the people of Limhi, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 20
s: The Lamanite attack occurs because the Lamanites believe the people of Limhi abducted their daughters. The people of Limhi defeat the attackers and capture their wounded king.

l: pacification, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 20
s: Pacification occurs when Limhi explains that the priests abducted the daughters. The king of the Lamanites and his people then meet the people of Limhi without arms and return peacefully.

l: the people of Limhi’s defense, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 20
s: The people of Limhi use waiting places in the fields and forests to attack the Lamanites. Although fewer in number, they fight for their lives, wives, and children and drive the Lamanites before them.

l: The Book of Mosiah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 21
s: Limhi and the people of Limhi return to the city of Nephi but suffer oppression, afflictions, failed battles, and bondage under the Lamanites. After humbling themselves and crying to God, they begin to prosper, and the Lord softens the Lamanites’ hearts so their burdens are eased, though they are not yet delivered. Ammon and his brethren arrive from Zarahemla, and Limhi learns that king Mosiah can interpret the record brought from a destroyed land covered with dry bones. Limhi and many of his people covenant with God and desire baptism, but Ammon declines to perform it because he considers himself unworthy and lacks authority.

l: Limhi, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 21
s: Limhi returns with his people to the city of Nephi and grants their request to battle the Lamanites. He later commands support for the widows and their children, sends men to search for Zarahemla, welcomes Ammon and his brethren, and enters into a covenant with God while desiring baptism.

l: the people of Limhi, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 21
s: The people of Limhi suffer oppression, repeated defeats, mourning, hunger, and bondage under the Lamanites. They humble themselves, cry to God, begin to prosper, enter into a covenant with God, and desire baptism.

l: Lamanites, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 21
s: The Lamanites become stirred up against the Nephites, impose heavy burdens, smite and drive the people of Limhi, and defeat them in battle. Their hearts are later softened so that they ease the burdens of Limhi’s people.

l: Nephites, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 21
s: The Nephites in this unit are the people of Limhi, who are surrounded, afflicted, and oppressed by the Lamanites. They suffer repeated military defeats and loss of life.

l: land of Lehi-Nephi, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 21
s: The city of Nephi is where Limhi and his people return and dwell. The people of Limhi return there after their failed battles, and Limhi is taken there after Ammon and his brethren are discovered.

l: land of Nephi, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 21
s: The land of Nephi is where Limhi’s people dwell under Lamanite oppression. Men sent to search for Zarahemla return to this land after finding a destroyed, peopled land.

l: priests of Noah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 21
s: The priests of Noah have fled into the wilderness, stolen the daughters of the Lamanites, and caused great destruction. Limhi’s people seek to capture and punish them, and the priests have also stolen grain and precious things.

l: king Noah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 21
s: Noah is identified as the king whose priests caused the people to commit many sins and iniquities against God. His priests are associated with the destruction involving the Lamanites.

l: Ammon, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 21
s: Ammon and his brethren come from Zarahemla and are initially mistaken for the priests of Noah, so they are bound and imprisoned. Ammon rejoices at learning that king Mosiah can interpret the engravings, mourns the deaths and departures of their people, and declines to baptize Limhi’s people because he considers himself an unworthy servant.

l: Ammon's brethren, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 21
s: Ammon’s brethren come with him from Zarahemla and are initially bound and cast into prison after being mistaken for the priests of Noah. They mourn the deaths caused by Noah and his priests and the departure of Alma and the people who went with him.

l: Zarahemla, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 21
s: Zarahemla is the land from which Ammon and his brethren come. Men sent by Limhi to find it cannot locate it and become lost in the wilderness.

l: king Mosiah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 21
s: King Mosiah has a gift from God that allows him to interpret engravings.

l: Alma, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 21
s: Alma forms a church of God through the strength and power of God and faith in the words spoken by Abinadi, then flees into the wilderness with his people. Ammon and his brethren mourn Alma’s departure, and Limhi’s people desire to become like Alma and his brethren.

l: Alma's brethren, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 21
s: The people who went with Alma flee into the wilderness with him after forming a church of God. Ammon and his brethren mourn their departure, and Limhi’s people desire to become like them.

l: Abinadi, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 21
s: Abinadi’s words are associated with the formation of Alma’s church of God. Ammon and his brethren mourn his death.

l: church of God, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 21
s: The church of God is formed by Alma and the people who went with him through the strength and power of God and faith in Abinadi’s words. Limhi’s people desire to form themselves into a church but wait upon the Spirit of the Lord because no one in the land has authority to baptize.

l: discovered land of the destroyed people, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 21
s: The destroyed land covered with dry bones was once peopled and had been destroyed. Men sent by Limhi find it, suppose it to be Zarahemla, and return with a record of its people.

l: record of the destroyed people, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 21
s: The record of the destroyed people is brought back on plates of ore by the men who found the destroyed land. Limhi learns that king Mosiah can interpret its engravings.

l: battles against the Lamanites, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 21
s: Limhi’s people go against the Lamanites three times after complaining of their afflictions. They are beaten and driven back each time, suffering much loss and many deaths.

l: destruction of Limhi's people, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 21
s: The destruction of Limhi’s people includes many men being slain in battle, leaving a great number of widows and causing mourning and lamentation throughout the land.

l: bondage, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 21
s: Limhi’s people are surrounded and subjected to the Lamanites’ authority, burdens, blows, and driving. They humble themselves and submit to the yoke of bondage, while the Lord later eases their burdens without yet delivering them.

l: afflictions of the Nephites, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 21
s: The afflictions of the Nephites are great because the Lamanites surround them on every side and there is no way for them to deliver themselves. Their afflictions lead them to murmur, battle, humble themselves, and cry to God.

l: covenant, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 21
s: Ammon and his brethren have entered into a covenant with God to serve him and keep his commandments. Limhi and many of his people also enter into a covenant with God.

l: baptism, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 21
s: Limhi and many of his people desire baptism as a witness and testimony that they are willing to serve God with all their hearts. Baptism is postponed because no one in the land has authority from God, and Ammon declines to perform it.

l: gift from God to interpret engravings, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 21
s: The gift from God to interpret engravings is possessed by king Mosiah. Ammon tells Limhi about this gift, which allows Mosiah to interpret the engravings on the plates of ore.

l: deliverance from bondage, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 21
s: Limhi’s people cry mightily to God for deliverance from their afflictions and bondage. The Lord eases their burdens by softening the hearts of the Lamanites, but does not yet deliver them from bondage.

l: The Book of Mosiah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 22
s: Ammon and king Limhi consult the people of Limhi about escaping bondage, but they find no way to fight the numerous Lamanites. Gideon proposes sending wine to the Lamanites so their guards will become drunk, allowing the people of Limhi to escape through a secret pass by night. The people of Limhi depart with their families, flocks, herds, provisions, and precious things, travel through the wilderness around the land of Shilom, and reach the land of Zarahemla. Mosiah receives them as subjects, while the Lamanites pursue them but become lost in the wilderness.

l: Ammon, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 22
s: Ammon consults with king Limhi and the people of Limhi about how they should deliver themselves out of bondage. He leads the people of Limhi and his brethren toward the land of Zarahemla.

l: Limhi, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 22
s: king Limhi consults with the people about delivering themselves from bondage and listens to Gideon's plan. He sends wine and more wine as a present to the Lamanites, then leads his people in departing by night.

l: Gideon, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 22
s: Gideon proposes using wine to make the Lamanite guards drunk and escaping through a secret pass behind the city. He offers to pay the last tribute of wine and says he will deliver the people from bondage.

l: the people of Limhi, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 22
s: The people of Limhi gather their flocks and herds, depart by night with their women and children, and take their provisions, gold, silver, and precious things. They travel through the wilderness to the land of Zarahemla, join Mosiah’s people, and become his subjects.

l: Lamanites, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 22
s: The Lamanites are numerous and hold the people of Limhi in bondage. Their guards drink freely of the wine sent by king Limhi, and the Lamanites later pursue the departing people for two days before becoming lost in the wilderness.

l: land of Shilom, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 22
s: The people of Limhi travel around the land of Shilom in the wilderness during their escape.

l: Zarahemla, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 22
s: The people of Limhi arrive in the land of Zarahemla after many days in the wilderness and join Mosiah’s people there.

l: the wilderness, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 22
s: The people of Limhi travel through the wilderness with their families, flocks, herds, provisions, and precious things. The Lamanites pursue them into the wilderness but lose their tracks and become lost.

l: bondage, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 22
s: The people of Limhi consult about how to deliver themselves out of bondage under the Lamanites. Gideon offers a plan that enables them to depart from it.

l: deliverance from bondage, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 22
s: Ammon, king Limhi, and the people of Limhi seek deliverance from bondage but cannot achieve it by contending with the Lamanites by the sword. Gideon’s plan uses wine and a secret pass to deliver the people through escape.

l: the escape of the people of Limhi, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 22
s: The escape of the people of Limhi occurs by night after the Lamanites drink the wine sent by king Limhi. The people travel around the land of Shilom through the wilderness and reach the land of Zarahemla.

l: the journey to Zarahemla, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 22
s: The journey to Zarahemla takes the people of Limhi many days through the wilderness. They are led by Ammon and his brethren and arrive with their families, herds, flocks, provisions, and precious things.

l: The Book of Mosiah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 23
s: Alma leads his people into the wilderness, where they establish the land and city of Helam and prosper. Alma teaches them to reject kingship, love one another, and accept only just teachers and ministers. The Lord later softens the Lamanites’ hearts, but the Lamanites take possession of Helam and place Alma’s people under guards. Amulon and the priests of king Noah join the Lamanites and receive authority over people in Helam.

l: Alma, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 23
s: Alma leads his people away from the armies of king Noah and into the wilderness. He teaches them about liberty, rejects kingship, serves as their high priest, consecrates just priests and teachers, and encourages them to trust the Lord when the Lamanites appear.

l: Lord, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 23
s: The Lord warns Alma, strengthens his people so they cannot be overtaken, softens the hearts of the Lamanites, and later delivers Alma’s people from bondage.

l: God, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 23
s: God delivers Alma’s people from the hands of king Noah and his people and from the bonds of iniquity. Alma teaches that God can deliver them from the Lamanites.

l: king Noah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 23
s: King Noah and his priests oppress Alma’s people, hold them in bondage, and bring them into iniquity. His armies pursue Alma’s people but cannot overtake them.

l: Amulon, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 23
s: Amulon leads the priests of king Noah and pleads with the Lamanites for their lives. He joins the Lamanites and is granted power to be a king and ruler over his people in the land of Helam.

l: Alma's brethren, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 23
s: The people of Alma flee from king Noah, settle in a beautiful land, and build the land and city of Helam. They prosper, are captured by the Lamanites, and are placed under guards.

l: this people, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 23
s: The people of king Noah pursue Alma’s people but cannot overtake them. They are associated with the oppression and bondage suffered by Alma’s people.

l: priests of Noah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 23
s: The priests of king Noah oppress Alma’s people and bring them into iniquity. Led by Amulon, they join the Lamanites and begin to possess and till the land of Amulon.

l: Lamanites, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 23
s: The Lamanites take possession of the land of Helam after the Lord softens their hearts. They promise Alma’s people liberty for directions to the land of Nephi, but break the promise and set guards over them.

l: the brethren of Alma, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 23
s: The brethren of Alma flee from their fields when the Lamanites appear and gather in the city of Helam. They pray for mercy, surrender to the Lamanites, and become subject to their guards.

l: the land of Helam, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 23
s: The land of Helam is a beautiful and pleasant land with pure water where Alma’s people settle, till the ground, build, and prosper. The Lamanites later take possession of it.

l: the city of Helam, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 23
s: The city of Helam is built by Alma’s people in the land of Helam. Alma’s people gather there when the Lamanites appear.

l: wilderness, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 23
s: Alma’s people flee eight days into the wilderness before the armies of king Noah. The Lamanite armies that followed the people of king Limhi are lost in the wilderness for many days.

l: land of Nephi, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 23
s: The Lamanites travel in search of the land of Nephi after joining Amulon and the priests of king Noah. Some of them go to the land of Nephi after Alma shows them the way.

l: the bondage of king Noah and his priests, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 23
s: The bondage of king Noah and his priests oppresses Alma’s people and brings them into iniquity. Alma teaches that God delivers them from this bondage.

l: liberty, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 23
s: Alma teaches his people to stand fast in the liberty given by God and not to trust a king over them. The Lamanites promise Alma’s people their liberty but do not keep the promise.

l: bonds of iniquity, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 23
s: King Noah and his priests bring Alma’s people into iniquity. Alma says that God delivers them from the bonds of iniquity.

l: departure into the wilderness, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 23
s: The flight from king Noah begins after Alma is warned that Noah’s armies will come. Alma’s people gather their flocks and grain and flee eight days into the wilderness.

l: the deliverance of Alma’s people, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 23
s: The deliverance of Alma’s people includes their escape from king Noah, their release from the bonds of iniquity, and the Lord’s later deliverance from bondage. The Lord shows his mighty power to them, causing great rejoicing.

l: the Lamanite capture of Helam, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 23
s: The Lamanite capture of Helam occurs after the Lord softens the Lamanites’ hearts and Alma and his brethren surrender. The Lamanites take possession of the land and set guards over Alma and his brethren.

l: The Book of Mosiah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 24
s: Amulon gains favor with king Laman and appoints the brethren of Amulon as teachers over the Lamanites, but they teach worldly skills rather than the things of God. Amulon exercises authority over Alma and his people, persecutes them, and places them under harsh tasks and guards. God lightens their burdens, promises deliverance, and leads Alma and his people out of bondage into the wilderness. After twelve days, Alma and his people arrive in the land of Zarahemla, where Mosiah receives them with joy.

l: Amulon, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 24
s: Amulon gains favor with king Laman and exercises authority over Alma and his brethren. He persecutes them, causes their children to persecute Alma’s people’s children, and puts tasks and task-masters over them.

l: brethren of Amulon, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 24
s: The brethren of Amulon are appointed as teachers over the Lamanites in several lands. They teach the language of Nephi, record keeping, and writing, but do not teach about God, the law of Moses, or the words of Abinadi.

l: Lamanites, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 24
s: The Lamanites possess the lands of Shemlon, Shilom, and Amulon and are ruled by appointed kings. They learn the language of Nephi, increase in riches, trade, and become cunning and wise in the wisdom of the world, while delighting in wickedness and plunder except among their own brethren. Their task-masters pursue Alma and his people, but God causes the Lamanites and their task-masters to sleep and later stops their pursuit.

l: king Laman, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 24
s: Laman is king of the Lamanites and is named after his father. He rules over a numerous people and appoints teachers in the lands possessed by his people.

l: God, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 24
s: God hears Alma and his people in their afflictions, promises to deliver them from bondage, and eases their burdens. God causes the Lamanites to sleep, leads Alma’s people out of bondage, and stops the Lamanites from pursuing them in the valley.

l: Alma, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 24
s: Alma is one of the king’s priests who believed the words of Abinadi and was driven out before the king. He leads his people out of bondage into the wilderness, and God tells him that He will go with him.

l: Alma's people, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 24
s: Alma’s people suffer persecution, tasks, task-masters, and guards under Amulon. They pour out their hearts to God, bear their burdens with ease after God strengthens them, depart into the wilderness, give thanks, and arrive in the land of Zarahemla.

l: afflictions, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 24
s: The afflictions of Alma and his people become so great that they cry mightily to God. Their afflictions are the setting in which God visits them, strengthens them, and promises deliverance.

l: covenant, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 24
s: God knows of the covenant Alma and his people have made unto Him. He promises to covenant with His people and deliver them out of bondage.

l: burdens, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 24
s: The burdens laid upon Alma and his brethren are made light by God. God strengthens them so that they can bear their burdens with ease even while in bondage.

l: the bondage of king Noah and his priests, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 24
s: Alma and his people are held in bondage under Amulon and his task-masters. God delivers them from bondage and leads them into the wilderness.

l: wilderness, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 24
s: Alma and his people depart into the wilderness after escaping bondage. They travel for twelve days before arriving in the land of Zarahemla.

l: valley Alma, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 24
s: Alma and his people camp in a valley after traveling through the wilderness and call it the valley Alma because Alma led their way. There they give thanks to God, and God tells Alma to leave because the Lamanites are pursuing them.

l: land of Zarahemla, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 24
s: After being in the wilderness for twelve days, Alma and his people arrive in the land of Zarahemla. King Mosiah receives them with joy.

l: Zarahemla, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 24
s: Zarahemla is the land where Alma and his people arrive after twelve days in the wilderness.

l: Mosiah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 24
s: King Mosiah receives Alma and his people with joy when they arrive in the land of Zarahemla.

l: The Book of Mosiah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 25
s: King Mosiah gathered the people of Nephi and the people of Zarahemla and caused the records of Zeniff and the account of Alma and his brethren to be read. The people felt joy for those delivered from bondage, sorrow for those slain by the Lamanites, gratitude for God's goodness and power, and anguish for the Lamanites. Alma preached repentance and faith on the Lord, baptized king Limhi and his people, and established churches throughout the land of Zarahemla. The churches were united as the church of God, and the Lord poured out his Spirit upon the people.

l: king Mosiah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 25
s: King Mosiah gathered the people, caused the records of Zeniff and the account of Alma and his brethren to be read, spoke to the people, and granted Alma power to establish churches and ordain priests and teachers.

l: the people of Nephi, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 25
s: The people of Nephi were gathered with the people of Zarahemla in two bodies and were fewer in number than the Lamanites.

l: the people of Zarahemla, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 25
s: The people of Zarahemla were gathered with the people of Nephi, were more numerous than the descendants of Nephi, and were numbered with the Nephites.

l: Lamanites, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 25
s: The Lamanites were more numerous than the people of Nephi and the people of Zarahemla. The people felt sorrow and anguish for the Lamanites because of their sinful and polluted state.

l: the people, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 25
s: The people were gathered, heard the records read, and experienced joy, sorrow, gratitude, and anguish. They were taught repentance and faith, and many joined the churches of God.

l: the records of Zeniff, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 25
s: The records of Zeniff were read to the people, covering the time the people of Zeniff left the land of Zarahemla until they returned.

l: Zarahemla, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 25
s: The land of Zarahemla contained the people of Nephi and the people of Zarahemla, and Alma was granted power to establish churches throughout it.

l: Alma, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 25
s: Alma preached repentance and faith on the Lord, taught the people of Limhi and his brethren to remember the Lord's deliverance, baptized Limhi's people, and received power to establish churches and ordain priests and teachers.

l: Alma's brethren, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 25
s: Alma's brethren were delivered from the hands of the Lamanites and from bondage, and their account and afflictions were read to the people.

l: bondage, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 25
s: Those delivered from bondage were remembered with great joy, and Alma taught the people of Limhi and his brethren to remember that the Lord delivered them.

l: God, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 25
s: The people gave thanks to God for his immediate goodness and power in delivering Alma and his brethren from the Lamanites and from bondage.

l: the children of Amulon and his brethren, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 25
s: The children of Amulon and his brethren were displeased with the conduct of their fathers and took upon themselves the name of Nephi so they could be numbered among the Nephites.

l: the kingdom, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 25
s: The kingdom was conferred only upon those who were descendants of Nephi.

l: Limhi, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 25
s: King Limhi desired to be baptized, and Alma baptized him.

l: the people of Limhi, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 25
s: The people of Limhi desired to be baptized, and Alma baptized them after the manner he had baptized his brethren in the waters of Mormon.

l: church of God, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 25
s: The baptized people belonged to the church of God because of their belief on the words of Alma. Although there were many churches, they were all one church, the church of God.

l: churches, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 25
s: Alma established churches throughout the land of Zarahemla, with priests and teachers over each church. The churches taught repentance and faith in God and were united as one church.

l: the name of Christ, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 25
s: Those desirous to take upon themselves the name of Christ joined the churches of God and were called the people of God.

l: Christ, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 25
s: The people who desired to take upon themselves the name of Christ joined the churches of God.

l: Spirit of the Lord, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 25
s: The Lord poured out his Spirit upon the people of God, and they were blessed and prospered in the land.

l: repentance, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 25
s: Alma preached repentance to the people, and nothing was preached in the churches except repentance and faith in God.

l: faith in God, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 25
s: The churches preached faith in God, and the people were taught repentance and faith.

l: Lord, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 25
s: The Lord delivered Alma and his brethren from the hands of the Lamanites and from bondage. Alma taught the people to remember this deliverance, and the Lord poured out his Spirit upon the people of God.

l: the deliverance of Alma’s people, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 25
s: The people who had been delivered from bondage were a source of exceedingly great joy, and Alma taught them to remember that the Lord delivered them.

l: the reading of the records, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 25
s: King Mosiah caused the records of Zeniff and the account of Alma and his brethren to be read, and the people responded with wonder, joy, sorrow, gratitude, and anguish.

l: baptism, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 25
s: Alma baptized king Limhi and all his people who desired baptism, after the manner he had baptized his brethren in the waters of Mormon.

l: the establishment of churches, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 25
s: King Mosiah granted Alma power to establish churches throughout the land of Zarahemla and to ordain priests and teachers over every church.

l: preaching repentance and faith, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 25
s: Alma preached repentance and faith on the Lord, and the priests preached the word as it was delivered to them by Alma. The churches preached only repentance and faith in God.

l: The Book of Mosiah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 26
s: The rising generation does not believe the traditions of their fathers, including teachings about the resurrection and the coming of Christ, and many refuse baptism and church membership. Dissensions and flattering words lead some church members into sin, so Alma brings them before King Mosiah and then inquires of the Lord about how to judge them. The Lord confirms Alma’s authority, explains that the church is his, and commands that those who repent and confess their sins be forgiven and received, while those who will not repent are excluded. Alma records and applies the Lord’s commandments, after which the church has peace, prospers, and continues teaching and baptizing.

l: rising generation, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 26
s: The rising generation cannot understand the words of king Benjamin because they were little children when he spoke. They do not believe the traditions of their fathers, including the resurrection of the dead and the coming of Christ, and they refuse baptism and church membership.

l: Christ, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 26
s: The rising generation does not believe concerning the coming of Christ.

l: word of God, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 26
s: Because of their unbelief, the rising generation cannot understand the word of God, and their hearts are hardened. Alma and his fellow laborers teach the word of God and admonish people according to their sins.

l: people who believed Alma, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 26
s: The church admonishes members who commit sin and brings them before the priests and Alma. Alma regulates its affairs according to the word of the Lord; the church then has peace, prospers, receives many, and baptizes many.

l: people of God, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 26
s: The people of God are not initially as numerous as the separate unbelieving people, but dissensions cause the unbelieving group to become more numerous.

l: Mosiah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 26
s: Mosiah reigns when the unbelieving people increase through dissensions among the brethren. He has given Alma authority over the church and declines to judge the accused, delivering them into Alma’s hands.

l: sin, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 26
s: Flattering words cause some church members to commit many sins. Those who confess their sins and repent may be forgiven, while those who refuse to confess and repent are not numbered among the church.

l: Alma, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 26
s: Alma is the high priest and has authority over the church from king Mosiah. He inquires of the Lord about judging transgressors, records the Lord’s words, judges the accused, and regulates the affairs of the church.

l: Lord, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 26
s: The Lord answers Alma after Alma pours out his whole soul and confirms Alma’s blessings, authority, and covenant of eternal life. The Lord declares that those who hear his voice are his sheep, commands judgment and forgiveness according to repentance, and says that those who will not hear or repent will not be received among his people.

l: the founding of the church, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 26
s: Alma is blessed because he established a church among the people. The Lord says the church and its people shall be established and shall be his people.

l: transgressors, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 26
s: Transgressors are to be judged according to the sins they have committed. Those who confess their sins and repent sincerely are to be forgiven and received, while those who will not repent are not to be numbered among the people.

l: repentance, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 26
s: The church is for those baptized unto repentance, and those received must believe in the Lord’s name. Whoever repents sincerely after transgressing may be forgiven, while those who will not repent are excluded from the Lord’s people.

l: forgiveness, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 26
s: The Lord freely forgives those who are received into the church and believe in his name. He commands his people to forgive one another when a neighbor says that he repents, and says that those who refuse to forgive are under condemnation.

l: The Book of Mosiah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 27
s: Persecutions by unbelievers caused the church of God to complain, leading king Mosiah to prohibit persecution and command equality, humility, and self-support. Alma (son) and the sons of Mosiah secretly sought to destroy the church, but the angel of the Lord appeared, rebuked Alma, and called him to repentance. After fasting and prayer, Alma recovered his strength, declared that he had been born of God and redeemed, and began preaching the word of God with the sons of Mosiah. They traveled throughout the land, repaired injuries done to the church, and brought many people to the knowledge of the truth and their Redeemer.

l: church of God, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 27
s: The church of God suffered persecution and dissension from unbelievers, but king Mosiah commanded that it not be persecuted. Alma (son) and the sons of Mosiah later sought to destroy it, then worked to repair the injuries they had done to it.

l: unbelievers, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 27
s: Unbelievers inflicted persecutions on the church and caused many people to be led astray. They later persecuted Alma (son) and those with him while they preached the word of God.

l: persecutions, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 27
s: Persecutions inflicted by unbelievers became so great that the church complained to its leaders. King Mosiah then issued a proclamation against such persecution.

l: Alma (father of Alma the younger), The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 27
s: Alma (father) laid the church’s complaint before king Mosiah and prayed with much faith that Alma (son) would come to a knowledge of the truth. He rejoiced when Alma (son) was brought to him after the angelic appearance and gathered people to witness what the Lord had done.

l: king Mosiah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 27
s: King Mosiah consulted with his priests and sent a proclamation that unbelievers should not persecute members of the church of God. He also commanded equality, humility, and labor for support throughout the churches.

l: people, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 27
s: The people experienced peace, became numerous, scattered throughout the land, and built cities and villages. Many were led astray by Alma (son), but later Alma and the sons of Mosiah taught and brought many to the knowledge of the truth.

l: Lord, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 27
s: The Lord visited and prospered the people. He heard the prayers of his people and Alma (father), sent the angel of the Lord to Alma (son), and redeemed Alma (son) after his repentance.

l: God, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 27
s: God’s power was shown when the angel’s voice shook the earth and when Alma (son) was converted. Alma (son) taught that people must be born of God and become righteous to inherit the kingdom of God.

l: Alma the younger, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 27
s: Alma (son) was a wicked and idolatrous man who used flattery to lead people astray and sought to destroy the church of God. After the angel of the Lord rebuked him, he repented, was born of God and redeemed, and began preaching the word of God.

l: sons of Mosiah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 27
s: The sons of Mosiah were numbered among the unbelievers and secretly sought to destroy the church with Alma (son). After the angelic appearance, they confessed their sins, repaired injuries done to the church, preached the word of God, and brought many to the knowledge of the truth.

l: angel of the Lord, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 27
s: The angel of the Lord appeared to Alma (son) and those with him in a cloud, speaking with a voice like thunder that shook the earth. He rebuked Alma (son), testified of God’s power and authority, and commanded him to seek to destroy the church no more.

l: church persecution, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 27
s: Church persecution became severe enough that the church complained to its leaders. King Mosiah responded by forbidding unbelievers from persecuting members of the church of God.

l: prayers, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 27
s: The prayers of the people and of Alma (father) were heard by the Lord. The angel said that Alma (son) had been brought to the knowledge of the truth so that the prayers of the Lord’s servants might be answered according to their faith.

l: angelic appearance, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 27
s: The angelic appearance caused Alma (son) and those with him to fall to the earth in astonishment. Alma (son) became unable to speak or move until the people fasted and prayed for him.

l: fasting and prayer, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 27
s: The priests assembled and fasted and prayed for two days and two nights that Alma (son) would speak and regain the strength of his limbs. Afterward, his limbs received their strength and he began to speak.

l: conversion of Alma, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 27
s: The conversion of Alma occurred after the angel of the Lord confronted him about persecuting the church of God. Alma (son) repented, declared that he was born of the Spirit, and then taught others what he had experienced.

l: redemption, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 27
s: Alma (son) said that he had been redeemed of the Lord after repentance and tribulation. He described his soul as rescued from the gall of bitterness, bonds of iniquity, darkness, and eternal torment.

l: Redeemer, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 27
s: Alma (son) said that he had rejected his Redeemer but later came to know that the Redeemer would come and make himself manifest unto all. He taught that every knee would bow and every tongue confess before him.

l: Final Judgment, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 27
s: At the last day, all people will stand to be judged by the Redeemer. Those who live without God will confess that the judgment of everlasting punishment is just upon them and will tremble beneath his all-searching eye.

l: preaching the word of God, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 27
s: Alma and those who were with him traveled throughout the land preaching the word of God amid much tribulation and persecution. Their teaching consoled the church, confirmed its faith, and brought many to the knowledge of the truth.

l: Ammon, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 27
s: Ammon was one of the four sons of Mosiah who traveled through the lands under king Mosiah. He helped confess their sins, explain the prophecies and scriptures, and bring many to the knowledge of the truth.

l: truth, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 27
s: The angel of the Lord came to convince Alma (son) of the power and authority of God and bring him to the knowledge of the truth. Alma and the sons of Mosiah later taught the truth to those who desired to hear it.

l: the commandments of God, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 27
s: The angel commanded Alma (son) to seek to destroy the church no more, contrary to the commandments of God. Alma and those with him later exhorted the church to keep the commandments of God.

l: The Book of Mosiah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 28
s: The sons of Mosiah ask king Mosiah to let them go to the land of Nephi to preach the word of God among the Lamanites, and the Lord approves their request. They hope to bring the Lamanites to knowledge of the Lord, cure their hatred toward the Nephites, and help establish peace. King Mosiah translates the plates of gold with the interpreters, learning the history of the destroyed people and causing the people to mourn and gain knowledge. He then gives the records and interpreters to Alma the younger and commands him to preserve them and keep a record of the people.

l: sons of Mosiah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 28
s: The sons of Mosiah ask their father to let them go with selected companions to the land of Nephi to preach the word of God to the Lamanites. They desire the salvation of every creature and hope the Lamanites will abandon their hatred, rejoice in the Lord, and become friendly with the Nephites. The Lord promises to deliver them from the Lamanites, and king Mosiah grants their request.

l: king Mosiah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 28
s: King Mosiah asks the Lord whether he should let his sons preach among the Lamanites, and the Lord tells him to let them go. He translates the plates of gold with the interpreters, then gives the records and interpreters to Alma the younger and commands him to preserve them and keep a record of the people.

l: Lamanites, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 28
s: The Lamanites are the people among whom the sons of Mosiah go to preach the word of God. The sons of Mosiah hope to bring them to knowledge of the Lord, cure their hatred toward the Nephites, and help them become friendly with one another.

l: Lord, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 28
s: The Lord works upon the sons of Mosiah, who had been very vile sinners, and spares them in his infinite mercy. He tells king Mosiah to let his sons preach among the Lamanites, promising that many will believe and have eternal life and that the sons will be delivered from the Lamanites. He preserves the interpreters so that the iniquities and abominations of the people may be discovered.

l: land of Nephi, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 28
s: The sons of Mosiah request permission to go up to the land of Nephi to preach the things they have heard and impart the word of God to the Lamanites.

l: word of God, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 28
s: The sons of Mosiah desire to impart the word of God to the Lamanites and undertake a journey to preach it among them.

l: records, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 28
s: King Mosiah keeps and preserves the records according to the commandments of God. After translating the plates of gold, he gives the records and interpreters to Alma the younger and commands him to preserve them and keep a record of the people for future generations.

l: the plates of brass, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 28
s: King Mosiah takes the plates of brass among the records and things he has kept and preserved, and later confers them upon Alma the younger.

l: the plates of Nephi, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 28
s: King Mosiah takes the plates of Nephi among the records and things he has kept and preserved, and later confers them upon Alma the younger.

l: plates of gold, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 28
s: The plates of gold were found by the people of Limhi and delivered to king Mosiah by Limhi. King Mosiah translates their records with the interpreters, and the account causes his people to mourn exceedingly while giving them much knowledge.

l: interpreters, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 28
s: The interpreters are two stones fastened into the two rims of a bow and are used by king Mosiah to translate the records on the plates of gold. They are preserved by the Lord and later given by king Mosiah to Alma the younger.

l: Alma (father of Alma the younger), The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 28
s: Alma is identified as the father of Alma the younger, who receives the records and interpreters from king Mosiah.

l: Alma the younger, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 28
s: Alma the younger receives the plates of brass, the plates of Nephi, the records, and the interpreters from king Mosiah. He is commanded to keep and preserve them and to keep a record of the people, handing them down from one generation to another.

l: request to preach among the Lamanites, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 28
s: The sons of Mosiah plead with king Mosiah for many days to go to the land of Nephi with selected companions and preach the word of God among the Lamanites. King Mosiah asks the Lord about the request, receives permission, and grants it.

l: translation of the records, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 28
s: King Mosiah translates the records on the plates of gold by means of the interpreters. The translation gives an account of the people who were destroyed from the time of their destruction back to the building of the great tower and the creation of Adam, causing the people to mourn and giving them much knowledge.

l: The Book of Mosiah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 29
s: Mosiah asks the people whether they want a king, but after Aaron and Mosiah’s other sons decline the kingdom, he sends a written message explaining the dangers of kingship. The people accept Mosiah’s proposal to choose judges, and Alma becomes the first chief judge while peace continues through the land. Mosiah and Alma’s father die, and the reign of the kings ends as the reign of the judges begins among the Nephites.

l: Mosiah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 29
s: Mosiah asks the people whether they want a king and sends them a written message explaining the dangers of unrighteous kings. He remains king for the rest of his days, establishes judges, and dies in the thirty and third year of his reign at sixty and three years old.

l: Aaron, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 29
s: Aaron is named by the people as their desired king and ruler, but he has gone to the land of Nephi and will not take upon himself the kingdom.

l: people, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 29
s: The people first desire a king, then accept Mosiah’s arguments and choose judges. They become anxious that every person should have an equal chance and express willingness to answer for their own sins.

l: king, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 29
s: The people desire a king, but Mosiah teaches that an unrighteous king can cause iniquity, destruction, bondage, wars, and bloodshed. The people ultimately choose to have no king.

l: kingdom, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 29
s: The kingdom rightly belongs to Mosiah’s son, but he declines it, and none of Mosiah’s sons is willing to take it upon himself.

l: the voice of the people, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 29
s: The voice of the people first calls for Aaron to be king and later chooses judges. Mosiah teaches that the people should conduct their business by this voice.

l: contentions, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 29
s: Mosiah warns that appointing another king could cause contentions among the people, and that dethroning an iniquitous king requires much contention.

l: wars, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 29
s: Mosiah warns that disputes over kingship could cause wars, and he describes wars as part of the destruction caused by an unrighteous king.

l: bloodshed, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 29
s: Mosiah warns that contentions over kingship could cause much bloodshed and describes bloodshed as an effect of an unrighteous king.

l: peace, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 29
s: Mosiah has established peace throughout the land, and continual peace exists after Alma becomes chief judge.

l: judges, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 29
s: Mosiah proposes that judges be appointed to judge the people according to the law. The people appoint judges throughout the land, with higher and lower judges able to judge one another according to the voice of the people.

l: chief judge, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 29
s: Alma is appointed as the first chief judge and judges righteous judgments while keeping the commandments of God.

l: laws, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 29
s: Mosiah directs the people to be judged according to the laws given to their fathers, which he says are correct and were given by the hand of the Lord.

l: the commandments of God, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 29
s: Mosiah teaches that kings should establish and obey the commandments of God. He says that unrighteous kings can tear up and trample those commandments.

l: God, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 29
s: God is described as the source of just judgments and as one who delivers people from bondage when they humble themselves and cry mightily to him.

l: Lord, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 29
s: The Lord gives the laws to the fathers, and Mosiah commands the people to act in the fear of the Lord. The Lord’s mercy is extended to those who put their trust in him.

l: Alma, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 29
s: Alma is appointed the first chief judge and is also the high priest. He walks in the ways of the Lord, keeps the commandments, judges righteously, and presides during continual peace.

l: Nephites, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 29
s: The Nephites are the people among whom the reign of the judges begins throughout the land of Zarahemla.

l: land, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 29
s: The land is to be a land of liberty where people may enjoy their rights and privileges alike as long as the Lord permits them and their posterity to inherit it.

l: land of Zarahemla, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 29
s: The reign of the judges commences throughout the land of Zarahemla among the Nephites.

l: liberty, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 29
s: The people rejoice because liberty has been granted to them after they choose judges instead of a king.

l: equality among all men, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 29
s: Mosiah desires that inequality be no more in the land, especially among his people, and the people seek an equal chance throughout the land.

l: rights and privileges, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 29
s: Mosiah desires that every person may enjoy rights and privileges alike for as long as the Lord allows the people and their posterity to inherit the land.

l: sin, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 29
s: Mosiah teaches that without a king, the people will answer for their own sins and iniquities. Under an unrighteous king, the sins of many people are caused by the king’s iniquities.

l: reign of the judges, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 29
s: The reign of the judges begins throughout the land of Zarahemla after the people appoint judges, with Alma as the first and chief judge.

l: reign of the kings, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 29
s: The reign of the kings ends among the people of Nephi after the people relinquish their desire for a king.

l: appointment of judges, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 29
s: The people assemble throughout the land and cast their voices to appoint judges who will judge them according to the law.

l: Mosiah's written message, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 29
s: Mosiah’s written message explains the dangers and burdens of kingship, the problems caused by unrighteous kings, and the reasons to choose judges instead.

l: death of Mosiah, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 29
s: Mosiah dies in the thirty and third year of his reign at sixty and three years old, after the people have chosen judges.

l: end of the reign of the kings, The Book of Mosiah, Chapter 29
s: The reign of the kings ends after Mosiah’s message convinces the people to relinquish their desire for a king and appoint judges instead.

l: The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 1
s: After Mosiah’s death, Alma presides in the first year of the reign of the judges over the people of Nephi under Mosiah’s laws. Nehor preaches priestcraft, universal salvation, and support for priests, gains followers and wealth, establishes a church, and kills Gideon with a sword. Alma condemns Nehor, who acknowledges that his teachings opposed the word of God and is executed. Despite persecution and internal conflict, the church restores order, shares with the needy, prospers, and the people have peace through the fifth year of the reign of the judges.

l: Mosiah, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 1
s: Mosiah, the last king, dies after warring a good warfare and walking uprightly before God. He leaves no successor to reign, but he has established laws acknowledged by the people.

l: Alma, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 1
s: Alma reigns in the judgment-seat and judges Nehor according to the law. He condemns Nehor for priestcraft and for killing Gideon.

l: Nehor, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 1
s: Nehor preaches against the church, teaches that priests should be supported by the people, and declares that all mankind will have eternal life. He gains followers, money, and costly apparel, establishes a church, kills Gideon with a sword, acknowledges that his teachings oppose the word of God, and suffers an ignominious death.

l: Gideon, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 1
s: Gideon belongs to the church of God and is one of its teachers. He withstands Nehor with the words of God and is killed by Nehor’s sword.

l: God, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 1
s: God is associated with upright living, the church of God, and the word of God. The people of the church impart the word of God without money and without price.

l: people of Nephi, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 1
s: The people of Nephi acknowledge Mosiah’s laws and are obliged to abide by them. They experience persecution, conflict, prosperity, and peace, while the law is enforced against transgressors.

l: church of God, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 1
s: The church of God takes Nehor before Alma after Gideon is killed. Its members endure persecution, restore order, labor, share their substance with the needy, and become prosperous.

l: priests, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 1
s: Priests leave their labor to impart the word of God, after which they return diligently to their labors. They do not esteem themselves above their hearers, and the preacher is described as no better than the hearer.

l: law of Mosiah, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 1
s: The law established by Mosiah is acknowledged by the people and governs their conduct. It punishes liars, thieves, robbers, and murderers, and is applied to transgressors when possible.

l: word of God, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 1
s: The word of God is used by Gideon to withstand Nehor and by Alma in condemning priestcraft. It is imparted by the priests and by church members without money and without price.

l: priestcraft, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 1
s: Priestcraft is introduced among the people through Nehor’s preaching and pursuit of support, riches, and honor. Alma says that enforcing it by the sword would bring the people’s entire destruction, but it continues to spread through false doctrines.

l: persecution, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 1
s: People who do not belong to the church of God persecute its members with words because of their humility and free sharing of the word of God. Some church members also contend with adversaries and one another, causing affliction and trial.

l: reign of the judges, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 1
s: The reign of the judges begins after Mosiah’s death, with Alma in the judgment-seat. The unit describes events from its first year through peace among the people until its fifth year.

l: death of Gideon, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 1
s: Gideon, being advanced in years and unable to withstand Nehor’s blows, is slain by the sword. Nehor is then taken by the people of the church and brought before Alma.

l: execution of Nehor, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 1
s: Nehor is condemned according to the law acknowledged by the people. He is carried to the top of hill Manti, acknowledges that his teachings oppose the word of God, and suffers an ignominious death.

l: peace, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 1
s: The church begins to have continual peace again after its members remain steady, labor, and share with the needy. There is much peace among the people of Nephi until the fifth year of the reign of the judges.
